intro: Rosetta sites are the localized WordPress.org sites at xx.wordpress.org. They began in September 2007 as a way for translation teams to publish a localized download and a blog without building release packages by hand, and grew into a network that can also hold a locale's support forums, HelpHub articles, team P2 and handbook. Everything below cites a primary source; where the record is unclear or could not be reached, it says so.

paragraphs.text: WordPress gained gettext-based internationalization in version 1.2, and in February 2005 the project announced the wp-polyglots mailing list to coordinate translations and "pre-localized versions of WordPress available for download". Translators committed their files to the i18n Subversion repository and assembled localized download archives themselves.

On 10 September 2007 Nikolay Bachiyski asked the wp-polyglots list for beta testers of "official local WordPress sites". Each team would get a wordpress.org subdomain, a WordPress blog for installation instructions and news in its language, and "an interface for building and releasing your localized releases", so download archives no longer had to be built by hand. The working example was bg.wordpress.org.

Three days later Matt Mullenweg described what each site contained: a one-page info site with the essential parts of WordPress.org, a blog, forums tied to the WordPress.org user system, and a pre-localized download. He also wrote that the forums and sites "should be combined", which took another nine years.

On 30 September 2007 Bachiyski announced that "the beta-testing of the locale sites is over", thanked the French, Japanese, Indonesian and Turkish testers, and listed the setup steps for any team: choose a subdomain, give the locale code, name the administrators, conform the SVN repository to the Codex layout, and translate the theme's rosetta.pot file. That is the earliest dated use of the name "rosetta" for this system in the record. The WP20 book places the first Rosetta site, Bulgarian, in 2008; the mailing list shows bg.wordpress.org running a year earlier.

The Polyglots handbook explains the name: Rosetta is "the code name of the theme for the local WordPress sites", and "the name was inspired from the ancient Rosetta Stone, which contained more or less the same text in three different languages". No primary source records who chose it.

sections.heading: Separate install to shared network (2010 to 2014)

paragraphs.text: For its first seven years Rosetta was a separate WordPress install that shared user accounts with WordPress.org. In December 2010 the locale sites still ran the WordPress 2.9 branch and the original theme; in July 2011 Andrew Nacin moved their menus and header screenshots onto core's Menus and Custom Header features; a new design for all Rosetta sites appeared in April 2013. Translation moved from hand-edited files to GlotPress at translate.wordpress.org from 2010.

In March 2014 the Rosetta theme was imported into the public Meta Subversion repository under global.wordpress.org, followed by the plugins that run the sites. On 15 October 2014 the Polyglots chat notes record that "Rosetta and .org installs are now merged"; a Meta commit the same day updated the "Rosetta bridge to reflect new network setup". The Meta handbook now describes the result as a WordPress Multisite network, the Global Network, where each locale can have a main site, a team P2 at /team and an optional support site at /support.

Language packs changed what the sites are for. WordPress 3.7 (October 2013) installed and updated language files automatically, and WordPress 4.0 (September 2014) added a language chooser to the installer that downloads a language pack on the fly. The Core team's plan for 4.0 kept the full localized package for first downloads from the locale site and used language packs for everything after. Community Summit notes from November 2014 found that most active communities used their Rosetta site only for that localized download, because editors could not extend it, and that Germany, France and Portugal had built external community sites instead.

sections.heading: Growing into a locale home (2015 to 2019)

paragraphs.text: From 2015 every Rosetta site got a localized theme and plugin directory, and the Meta team started importing directory plugins and themes into translate.wordpress.org so they could ship language packs. In July 2016 the old bbPress 1 forums at xx.forums.wordpress.org were upgraded and moved to xx.wordpress.org/support. In September 2016 a "Rosetta" plugin for managing sites in the global.wordpress.org network was committed, and in October 2016 Dominik Schilling announced team P2 sites at xx.wordpress.org/team for all 71 locales with a current release. Locale handbooks live under those team sites.

In 2017 the Polyglots team started a "Rosetta outreach" effort to build local editorial teams separate from translation teams, and the new support-forum theme reached Rosetta forums. In March 2018 the new About pages were rolled out across the network.

HelpHub, the end-user documentation, came to Rosetta sites in 2019. The Docs team proposed localizing it as a plugin on each locale's support site rather than through GlotPress; a meeting at WordCamp Europe in June 2019 agreed to activate it on selected sites, starting with ja.wordpress.org, with the English HelpHub as the source of truth. Trials on the Japanese and Serbian sites followed in July 2019. The feature chart above shows how far that rollout got.

The Polyglots handbook counted "over 200 locales" in August 2020, and the teams page lists 208 today, 203 of them with a Rosetta site. The handbook calls the sites "a sole official interface of WordPress for users who speak a language other than US English" and expects each to carry a front page with a download link, a blog, a showcase and a contact page. Posts on a Rosetta site also reach the dashboard news feed of every WordPress install running that language.

In August 2023 the block-based WordPress.org theme was made available to Rosetta sites, switched on per locale once its strings were translated. By June 2024, 16 sites had moved and the Meta team set 1 July 2024 to move the rest. Spot checks on 14 October 2026 (bg, de, fr, ja, ko, mn) found every one on the new theme.

Locale forums upgrade to bbPress 2 and move to xx.wordpress.org/support.

roles.name: Locale Manager
roles.description: Has every Editor capability on the Rosetta site plus adding, promoting and removing users, appointing General Translation Editors and releasing WordPress packages. Automatically an Editor on the team site.

roles.name: General Translation Editor (GTE)
roles.description: Validates translations on every project for one locale. Promoted by a Locale Manager, or by a Global Mentor when the locale has no active GTE.

roles.name: Project Translation Editor (PTE)
roles.description: Validates translations for specific projects in one locale, appointed by a GTE. Cross-Locale PTEs are accounts of plugin or theme authors that can import strings for their own projects in every locale.

roles.name: Global Mentor and Tech Lead
roles.description: Can administer every Rosetta site, assign Locale Managers and create new sites, forums and team sites in the Global Network.

roles.name: Forum Keymaster and HelpHub Manager
roles.description: Roles on a locale's support site, assigned when its forums or HelpHub are deployed.

roles.name: Getting a site
roles.description: A new team posts a request on the Polyglots P2 with the locale code, country code, plural forms, native language name and admin usernames. Global Mentors then create the site, any forums and the team site.
